title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–7)
hookLine: the first human is shaped from adamah, the earth, and given breath

lines: A POTTER, HANDS IN THE CLAY.
THE STORY STARTS AGAIN, CLOSE UP.
cards: A potter at a wheel, or a kid at the beach, hands wet, shaping something out of mud. It's close work: thumbs pressing, the maker bent right over the thing being made.
In the first chapter of Genesis, God makes the world from far away, by speaking. In the second, the camera comes down close. The story starts again, and God shapes a person, as it were, by hand.

teach.h: ADAMAH — THE GROUND. ADAM — THE EARTHLING.
teach.b: In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Listen to the Hebrew.
The ground is adamah. The human made from it is adam. At first adam isn't only a name; it's a word: the earthling, the one from the earth.
And formed is the verb for a potter's work. Then God breathes into the nostrils, face to face, the breath of life, nishmat chayim.
Neshamah, breath, is the same word Jews use for the soul. So the soul, in this picture, is a breath that came from very close.
The Talmud adds that the dust for the first human was gathered from the whole earth. Rashi gives a reason: so that wherever a person dies, the ground will take them in.
Every land can be home. A Hasidic teacher, Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa, told his students to carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket.
On one: for my sake the world was created, from the Mishnah on day twenty-four. On the other: I am but dust and ashes, Abraham's words to God on day eight.

teach.h: AND MAN BECAME A LIVING SOUL.
teach.b: When you feel too proud, reach for the dust. When you feel worthless, reach for the other pocket. The trick is knowing which one.
Earth and breath: in this teaching, both are true of a person, all the time.

how: Jews read the second creation story in the first Torah portion each autumn; each morning's prayers begin by thanking God for returning the soul, the neshamah, and the Hasidic teaching of the two pockets is often retold.

o: the earthling, shaped from the ground
a name that simply means the first man
the garden where the first person lived

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: adam is only a personal name in the story
at first it's a word: the one from adamah, the ground.
the Hebrew for breath is also the word for soul
neshamah: the soul as a breath from very close.
in chapter two, God makes the human by speaking, as in chapter one
this time God forms the human from dust, like a potter, and breathes in the breath of life.

games.q: you carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket: "for my sake the world was created" and "I am but dust and ashes." you're feeling proud. which do you reach for?
o: for my sake the world was created.
I am but dust and ashes.
games.why: the dust. and on a day you feel worthless, the other pocket. the trick is knowing which one you need.

practice: Put both feet flat on the floor and feel them press toward the ground you're made of. Then breathe in slowly through your nose, and notice the air coming in close, the way the story says the first breath did.
Feet, earth; nose, breath: stay with both.

wordCard.voice: Adam. The earthling, shaped from adamah, the ground, and given breath from very close.

carryVoice: Your line: earth and breath. Dust and a living soul, in one person. Until tomorrow.
